A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Learning-to-Measure and retain matching methods, experiments, and proofs. All pages and appendices were readable, and figures, tables, equations, and relocated material could be compared reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic regression, tabular classification, and MNIST experiments, including uncertainty, acquisition-performance, and adaptivity analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds lookahead, synthetic-to-real transfer, natural-missingness, gradient-estimation, and alternative meta-learning experiments.

M1.justification: v1 optimizes a greedy one-step acquisition loss. v2 adds a k-step lookahead objective and optimization through sampled acquisition trajectories, with a one-step-lookahead policy evaluated experimentally (Section 4.2 and Appendix A.5). This substantially extends the acquisition procedure; straight-through Gumbel–Softmax itself already appeared in v1.

E1.justification: v2 adds fully synthetic classification tasks with generated covariates and varying feature dimensions, interaction-rich BNN-Plan tasks, and transfer from synthetic covariates to real-world tasks. It also evaluates MIMIC contexts containing natural missingness, introducing patient-population and missingness shifts beyond v1's complete-case data with injected missingness.

E2.justification: The original MLP, GDFS, DIME, and DQN comparisons remain. v2 additionally evaluates a CNP-like attention-pooling model and its test-time-tuned variant (Figure 18), REINFORCE gradient estimation (Figure 17), and offline and semi-offline IPW estimators (Table 5). These substantially broaden the evaluated comparison methods.

E3.justification: The reported MIMIC test pool changes from 10,000 to 3,000, baseline features from three to five, and acquirable features from ten to fifteen. Metabric drops the listed age baseline and abcb1 feature, and its missingness changes from MAR to MCAR (dataset descriptions and Table 2). New planning experiments control encoder/predictor freezing, temperature 0.5, and four Monte Carlo samples; gradient studies introduce reference-gradient and estimation-budget protocols.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's context-length, missingness-rate, and adaptive-versus-static analyses, v2 adds controlled feature-synergy/lookahead tests, informative-feature precision and recall, synthetic-prior transfer and fine-tuning, natural-missingness stress tests, gradient-estimator sensitivity, and CNP adaptation ablations (Figures 5 and 12–18; Table 5). These examine substantial additional questions about mechanisms and robustness.

E5.justification: v1 already reports standard errors across 200 tasks in Figure 3. v2 retains this practice and additionally reports means and standard deviations across 50 sampled tasks for gradient-estimation experiments (Figure 17 and Table 5). Neither version specifies repeated-training seed counts; the additions describe task-level variability.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial lookahead, transfer, gradient-estimation, and meta-learning results. For example, Table 5 newly reports pathwise one-step bias norm 0.068 ± 0.037 using four samples. Existing acquisition and uncertainty curves also change, especially for MIMIC under its revised setting; Table 1 changes LOS prevalence from 34.12% to 44.90% and mortality from 3.48% to 8.67%. These are revised-setting results, not directly comparable performance gains.

T1.justification: v2 adds formal submodularity and adaptive-submodularity definitions and discusses their approximation guarantee (Appendix A.4), then derives a multi-step lookahead objective and gradient estimator (A.5). It also extends the blocked-policy optimality argument across missingness patterns and corrects the missing inner gradient in Equation 6. The original identification assumptions and greedy theorems remain.

C1.justification: v1 presents greedy meta-AFA as its algorithmic contribution. v2's introduction explicitly extends this contribution to both greedy and planning-based acquisition and claims the first demonstration of their joint meta-learning formulation across tasks. This broadens the central contribution while retaining the original claims about in-context adaptation and robustness.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations involving feature synergy, task-representation bottlenecks, prior mismatch, and IPW estimation variance. It explicitly qualifies natural-missingness results because both population and context–query distributions shift, and adds limitations concerning full cost-sensitive planning and scale. The adaptivity interpretation also changes: v1 Figure 13 emphasizes benefits for LOS and mortality, whereas v2 Figure 15 says such benefits are difficult to demonstrate.

D1.justification: v2 documents BNN-Plan generation, synthetic covariate sampling, planning-specific hyperparameters, CNP adaptation, and logistic-regression propensity estimation, and adds baseline runtimes in Table 3. The hardware and source-code link are retained. However, Section 4.3 says the predictor is held fixed while Appendix A.7.6 retains joint updates for default training, leaving a reproducibility ambiguity.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through CNP/MAML-style meta-learning, TabPFN and continued pretraining, and IPW policy-gradient comparisons. It adds relevant work including DIFA, Norcliffe et al., and an in-context RL survey, and introduces an explicit novelty claim spanning greedy and planning-based meta-AFA. Publication updates for retained works such as DIME are bibliographic changes rather than new research relationships.

P1.justification: The introduction, problem formulation, method explanations, and results narrative are extensively rewritten. v2 separates test-time acquisition, meta-training, and architecture into Sections 4.1–4.3, introduces thematic results subsections, and reorganizes the appendices. It also replaces the separate ethics/reproducibility statements with revised end matter and removes the LLM-use section.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout and redraws Figures 1 and 2. v1 Figure 3 is split between v2 Figures 3 and 9; v1 Figure 5 moves to Figure 11; and the two adaptivity figures merge into Figure 15. Numerous new analytical figures and runtime/gradient tables are added, and MIMIC plots and heatmaps expand to fifteen features.

improvement.justification: The controlled lookahead experiments, alternative meta-learning comparisons, gradient diagnostics, and synthetic-to-real and natural-missingness tests substantially strengthen evidence for design choices and applicability beyond v1's evaluations. Explicit qualifications about prior mismatch and distribution shifts also improve interpretation. Reporting weaknesses remain, including conflicting predictor-freezing descriptions and apparently duplicated GP log-loss/MSE panels in Figures 4 and 10, but the added controls and substantive validation provide a clear substantial net improvement.
